Frost is a survival card game that understands how to make players feel hopeless in the most effective way possible. Set in a frozen world slowly being consumed by an endless winter, the game transforms survival into a constant battle against exhaustion, starvation, and inevitable collapse. Unlike many deckbuilding games that focus on empowering players with flashy combinations and increasingly powerful abilities, Frost takes the opposite approach. Every mechanic is designed to make survival feel fragile and temporary. Progress is not about becoming unstoppable but about delaying death for one more journey through the snow. That harsh philosophy gives the game a unique identity that separates it from almost every other survival deckbuilder on the market.

The core gameplay revolves around managing a group of survivors through card-based exploration and resource management. Every card represents something important, whether it is food, tools, weapons, injuries, ideas, or the survivors themselves. Players travel between locations by meeting card requirements while constantly balancing limited resources and trying to avoid complete collapse. At first, the mechanics seem manageable, but the game gradually introduces more pressure through fatigue, weather conditions, deck pollution, and difficult moral decisions. The further players progress, the more overwhelming the struggle becomes. Every successful move feels earned because the game rarely allows players to feel truly safe.

One of Frost’s greatest achievements is its atmosphere. The visual style perfectly captures the emotional emptiness of a dying frozen world. Nearly every environment is covered in pale white snow, faded blue shadows, and bleak grey ruins that create a constant sense of isolation. The artwork resembles dark illustrations from a post-apocalyptic storybook, with exhausted survivors wandering through endless storms searching for warmth that may not even exist anymore. The minimalist presentation works incredibly well because it allows the world to feel cold and lifeless without relying on excessive detail. The game’s environments rarely feel welcoming, and that emotional discomfort becomes one of the experience’s defining strengths.

The audio design contributes just as much to the atmosphere. Frost rarely uses dramatic or overwhelming music, instead relying on quiet ambient sounds, distant wind, and unsettling silence to create tension. The constant sound of snowstorms and harsh weather makes the environment feel hostile even during calm moments. Music appears only when necessary, and when it does, it reinforces the desperation and exhaustion that define the experience. The restrained soundtrack combined with the bleak visuals creates a remarkably immersive atmosphere that few survival games manage to achieve this effectively.

Mechanically, the game blends survival management with deckbuilding in creative ways. Every action affects the deck directly, meaning poor decisions can slowly poison future turns with useless or harmful cards. Hunger, injuries, exhaustion, and emotional strain all become physical obstacles within the deck itself, forcing players to constantly think about long-term survival instead of short-term victories. Building an efficient deck is not about creating unstoppable combinations but about reducing suffering and keeping the group functional for as long as possible. This creates a very different pacing from traditional roguelike deckbuilders where players usually become stronger over time.

The game’s scenario structure also adds a significant amount of replayability. Different missions introduce unique conditions, starting resources, and survival goals that force players to rethink their strategies constantly. Some scenarios become brutally difficult, demanding careful planning and efficient resource management from the very beginning. The game rewards adaptation and patience more than aggressive experimentation, which helps every successful run feel meaningful. Even failure often teaches players something valuable about resource priorities and deck efficiency.

One of the most interesting aspects of Frost is how emotionally draining it intentionally feels. The game constantly pressures players into uncomfortable decisions involving sacrifice, rationing, and survival at any cost. There are moments where keeping the group alive may require morally questionable actions, and the game never tries to make those choices feel heroic or satisfying. Instead, survival often feels desperate and exhausting. This emotional weight gives Frost a stronger psychological impact than many survival games that focus primarily on action or spectacle.

However, the game’s oppressive design can also become one of its biggest weaknesses. Frost is extremely unforgiving, especially for new players still learning how the systems interact. Early runs often end quickly and brutally, sometimes because of bad luck or unclear mechanics rather than obvious mistakes. The tutorials and explanations are limited considering how punishing the systems can become, forcing players to learn largely through repeated failure. Some players may appreciate this harsh learning curve, while others may simply find it frustrating.

The game’s pacing can also feel slow and mentally exhausting during longer sessions. Because every decision carries consequences, even relatively small actions require careful thought and planning. Combined with the bleak atmosphere, this creates an experience that can become emotionally draining over time. Frost is not designed for relaxed or casual gameplay sessions. It constantly demands focus, patience, and attention to detail, which may not appeal to players looking for faster or more rewarding progression systems.

Readability can occasionally become another issue. The muted art style and minimalist interface fit the atmosphere perfectly, but some cards and information can blend together visually during complex situations. While the presentation is beautiful in its own bleak way, it occasionally sacrifices clarity in favor of maintaining the oppressive aesthetic.

Despite these flaws, Frost succeeds because of how completely it commits to its vision. Every mechanic, visual element, and audio cue reinforces the feeling of surviving in a hopeless frozen world where every victory is temporary. The game never breaks its atmosphere for convenience or accessibility, and that commitment makes the experience feel far more immersive and emotionally memorable than many larger survival games.

For players who enjoy difficult strategy games, survival mechanics, and atmospheric deckbuilders, Frost offers a uniquely bleak and rewarding experience. It is harsh, exhausting, and unforgiving, but beneath that frozen exterior lies one of the most emotionally immersive survival card games available. Players willing to embrace its brutality will discover a deeply strategic and unforgettable journey through a world where hope slowly disappears beneath the snow.

It's quite interesting, if flawed here and there. It sucks that the game came out before the explosion of roguelike card battlers, I believe it would've been much more successful otherwise. It's designed in such a way that you could easily play a board game version if you wished to, and that's nice.

The objective is to reach the Refuge, which you do by completing a set amount of regions. In order to complete a region, you must "tap" (as in: use but not sacrifice from the deck) a given set of resources. You can only hold 5 cards at a time, so you have to figure out ways to draw more cards. And you do need to hurry up - the Frost is coming. Every turn you do not travel, you lose one point in the Frost counter. Luckily, when you travel the counter goes up by one. 

And that's pretty much the entire game in a nutshell. Keep that deck lean and powerful. As you unlock content, you'll have to deal with "events" - some dangers which require you either to use a specific card, sacrifice some resources, or lose either a hit point (you have 4 of those) or a survivor. Both are valuable, so be careful. Sadly, this is also where the game starts to get a little too RNGy - it feels like sometimes you just lose because you didn't have enough luck with the cards. But perhaps that's just because I'm not so good at it. That said, I managed to beat the game on Hard, and to me that's completion - I'm satisfied.

Another thing that could be different is the unlock system. To keep things short, you never know when you'll unlock things or what do you need to do to. I unlocked a few scenarios - beat them all - but I know there's far more, and I don't think there's much point in replaying this too much. Although I probably will return to this game every now and then, we'll see.

Overall - I recommend it if you're into card games. This is quite different from whatever offerings there are on roguelike deckbuilder market now, simply because this is mainly a resource management/survival game. If nothing else, you'll appreciate the fresh and creative design.

I don't like strategy/survival games generally because I find them tedious and frustratingly complex. This game is different. While it is quite simple in concept, it kept me engaged over many play throughs balancing challenge, atmosphere, and length quite well. It's the perfect kind of casual but engaging game, and I'm excited to keep playing and unlock more and more. Though I do recommend playing the demo first since it's available and a great test to see if you'll like this game.

Pros:
- The bits of story attached to the cards and intro I really enjoyed. 
- The art/atmospheric design: it is simple, but really well done in it's simplicity. It feels harsh and threatening and gets more so as the Frost gets closer.
- The harshness extends beyond the art/atmosphere into both the brutal randomness of the cards/deck and the lack of direction on how to unlock things further.
- Easy is still very much easy, but in a way that feels very rewarding when you've at some point had at least one very harsh round and got past it. Also if you get stuck it's easy to restart from the menu pulled up by escape, or just let yourself die and start over from the main menu.
- Custom mode lets you choose the difficulty by changing various options.

Cons: 
- There's no guidance on how to unlock cards or scenarios, but I do think it's designed to be that way, as it adds to the eerie harsh environment of the game.
- It fits the environment and theme but the brutal randomness might not be for you.
- While most of the icon/cards are pretty straight forward to figure out they would benefit from a description. For example, there's a speech bubble icon that I'm not entirely sure how to get or what it represents. 
- It can be confusing how the number of your resources change and how to figure out if you change them to get what you need. The game could benefited from more guidance on how the game plays out and how various cards work/work together. Though, it feels like it might intentional to add to the mystery, difficulty, and harshness.
- Due to the above-mentioned cons, there's a good argument for the game feeling like and early access or rushed/unfinished version. It doesn't bother me as it adds to the atmospheric harshness and the games not super expensive, but it's worth noting.

I keep coming back to this game - mostly on mobile/tablet. If you know what a deck-building game is (like Dominion, Ascension), this is a solitaire deck-builder that unlocks complexity over multiple plays. If that doesn't mean much to you, just know that it is not like a collectible card battler like the popular games, Hearthstone or physical Pokemon card game. Building and shaping the deck of cards you play with happens during the game (not between matches). So you are always deciding the costs of using up or trading cards while you try to survive the trip.

The theme is surprisingly strong. Individual faces on each person in your tribe can actually cause you to hesitate: Do I damage the tribe leader or sacrifice this face looking at me? The cannibalism card is just -- I almost never use it. I know it's just cards but the simple pervasive theme and mood just works on me and raises the game above a math problem or puzzle and makes it feel like a survival story.

Why it's not perfect:
The interface has had issues in the past and it is improved but it takes some getting used to. It would be nice if it was clearer how it worked and it can feel a bit clunky instead of intuitive, at first. On the plus side of this, it is smooth and quick once you get accustomed. 

It can feel a bit punishing, at first, because you may not realize how terrible your choices have been when you first begin. It's not always the randomness causing you to lose. ;)

An unfair randomness does creep into the odd game that can be frustrating -- especially when not many cards are unlocked/collected and temperature starts affecting how many cards you draw. However, if you can accept that some play just won't be fair or even possible, the decisions and different approaches to take are a fun mental ride. Also, after you play a bunch of solitaire games, you may begin to realize that it really has to be difficult and present impossible scenarios or it becomes quickly unsatisfying.

In my experience, running up against a brick wall did get me to try different approaches, and thanks to the additional cards earned, the complexity and depth of the game increases as you play over and over, so it keeps you learning for a long time.

I've had the game for years, and I must really like it because I keep going back for more. Recommended!

Frost is my favorite take on the deck-building genre yet. Most of these types of games emphasize the acqusition of new cards, where the decision making is all about what you add to your deck. Frost, however, has a ton of ways to remove cards from your deck, and it turns every game into a tense balancing act where your deck can rapidly fluctuate in size in a single turn.

The gameplay is simple enough: You have to gather resources to pass by region cards. Successful travels will tick up the Frost meter as you get further away from the storm, while stalling out will allow the Frost meter to tick down. Random event cards show up that can threaten or help you out, and special idea cards appear at each location for you to purchase and supplement your deck.

The gameplay is supplemented by the scenarios. Each one introduces a new character who has special abilities, but must also overcome some special scenario, like finding 4 pets by the end of the run, or beating a special enemy encounter. Completing a scenario unlocks that character for the main gameplay mode, but I think the scenarios are really the heart of Frost. They're all unique and enjoyable, and many even find clever ways to integrate storytelling into the card mechanics. For example, to drive home the Tracker's loneliness, you can find the Gathering card during her scenario, but you can never buy it, since she can't generate two survivors in a turn.

The game's presentation is solid. The scratchy art-style looks terrific, and the music is wonderfully moody. The localization is a bit rough in spots, but there's not a lot of text, so it's not a huge issue. The art is plain, scribbly, and weirdly fitting. I can't imagine it looking cleaner and still working this well.

You can't see the precise contents of decks or monitor discard piles of events and such like you could in a physical card game, so there's slightly more pressure on you that something bad might be just around the corner. 

Sources of cards all add to your singular deck, but you don't know the precise odds of a given source giving you something good or bad. Sending someone to scout? You can't do precise mathsy odds calculation of whether they'll die or add fatigue to your deck.

Unlocks mean the game gets broader and deeper. Scenarios challenge you to play under specific conditions for specific goals, and you can also tweak the rules and deck kindness to get an easier or harder game.

There's no scoring; there's just succeeding or dying.

I really liked a lot of what Frost was doing. The aesthetic is stylish, and I liked the minimalist sound design with snowy footsteps and tribal chants. The cards are well-designed, and perfectly fit thematically with the narrative. Although I feel that I never won more than 1/3 of the time, I always wanted to set out again for the refuge. I wanted to escape the Frost!

The refuge is found after travelling a certain number of times, perhaps 25 in a basic game. In order to travel, you need to pay the requirements of a location card. Each location card will require either food, wood, survivors, or some combination of the three. Each time you travel, you create distance between yourself and the Frost. Each turn you dawdle, the Frost grows ever closer. At each location, there is an event happening. Sometimes you can draw extra cards by spending food. Other times, you might run into a group of savages that want to kill your survivors. Attackers can be killed with weapons, but can kill one of your survivors or damage your health (you begin with 4 health) if not dealt with.

Instead of paying the cost of the location card, you can also use resources to buy special cards for your deck or send your survivors out to scavenge. These extra cards can help you do things such as get food more efficiently, heal your wounds, or fight adversaries. Survivors can find other people, pets, food, or wood, although sometimes they find nothing or die in the scavenging attempt. Scavenging failures, as well as certain events, can cause your group to become more fatigued. Fatigue cards clog your deck, and must be managed with purchased special cards or periodic rests (in which you skip a turn to remove all fatigue cards from your hand).

This all sounds quite complicated, and this is without even mentioning how temperature can affect hand size or how different playable characters have innate abilities. However, the game introduces you to these new concepts at a carefully measured rate. After each game, you unlock a new card or cards, and new events. Periodically, you'll also unlock new scenarios which you can conquer for extra playable characters. I never felt overwhelmed by the mechanics of the game, although they can be complicated. It can be very satisfying to think your way out of a bad situation by utilizing character abilities or special cards.

My first 8 hours with the game were fantastic. I continued playing until I unlocked all of the cards, and then beat the first four scenarios. However, things became a rough slog afterwards. The remaining scenarios are brutally difficult, and often seem to require a lot of luck. I would often feel that I was in a good position, but would be unable to seal the deal. On one occasion, I only needed one food card to proceed. I sent out six survivors to scavenge, and they all brought back wood. On four occasions, I lost "The Recruiter" scenario after travelling 19 times (out of 25). I felt that the difficulty of the events was out of sync with the strength of the cards I could purchase. After unlocking all of the cards, basic games also became much more difficult. One advanced event card in particular, traverse, kept popping up at the beginning of my games. This event causes the location card to remove all resources spent to travel from your deck. At the beginning of the game when you only possess perhaps 2 wood, 2 food, and 2 survivors, this is absolutely debilitating. During my last three hours with Frost, I didn't win a single game!

Barring the possibility that I suddenly lost all the proficiency I had gained during the first 8 hours of play, I think that there is an enormous RNG difficulty curve at the tail end of the game. I absolutely recommend the title, but think that after unlocking all of the cards and seeing all the mechanics, you've seen the best that the title has to offer.

Stark, soft, and beautiful, Frost is almost a great game. Its visuals, low-key world-building, atmospheric winter soundtrack, and general design aesthetic are fantastic. Its core gameplay is fun...but only until you scratch beneath the surface and realize that this is Gods Must Be Watching with a nicer face and prettier clothes.

The problem with Frost is that it's heavily, heavily randomized around its most basic mechanic. You have a hand of survivors, you use them to get resources and new survivors, and you spend your resources to keep ahead of the terrible everstorm at your back. Unfortunately, every time you send a survivor out to scavenge, there's a chance they come back with a featureless trash card and there's a chance they outright die. The game's pacing is relentless and requires highly skilled play...but even then, everything you do devolves back into luck.

Do you draw Fatigue cards or resources? Do your survivors die while scavenging? Do you get the right ideas, regions, or card combinations in your hand to be able to pass an obstacle in time? Are there the right cards available in your region?

Playing well helps you hedge your risks, but you can have starting turns where every one of your three survivors dies or draws Fatigue. Deck clog is a nightmare, and the game has a deck resource tracker that you are only allowed to use on easy mode: i.e. not during real play. On top of that, it has a number of mechanics that it doesn't actually show you. The temperature of a region determines how many cards you draw for each hand, but that temperature isn't clearly marked anywhere...except outside of easy mode. New cards and scenarios can be unlocked through play, but how the game decides when it's ready to give you one is utterly incomprehensible.

On top of that, the limited story of the game unfolds through those scenarios--specific challenges with unique deck mechanics and abilities designed to create a slightly different gamefeel--and unfortunately that gamefeel consists of constantly hammering on the restart button.

Let's take the first unlock, The Leader. You start with three survivors, one wood, two food, and four Fatigue. If one of those starting survivors dies, it's game over. You have an ability that lets you spend one food from your hand for a 50% shot at a new survivor. 50% it does nothing and consume the food. And depending on your start location, you'll need to pay a mix of food, wood, and survivors to get to the next location. Wait too long, and the everstorm murders you.

So, to get enough resources to even have a hope of getting ahead of the storm, you need to send those plot-critical survivors scavenging right out of the gate.

Which means in this particular scenario you'll get game-overed at random on the very first card you play about one time out of ten.

And that's only the most blatant way Frost screws you. As you get deeper into your runs and the everstorm gets closer, you'll end up in situations where you need a survivor to draw a single food to pass on to the next region and every survivor you send comes back with a tree. Two turns later, the storm eats you, all your trees are for naught.

Frost *is* fun, despite the fact that you will play perfectly and lose a lot of the time, but it's not quite what it could be.

If you want a Dominions-y CCG with rich story, deep gameplay, and minimal input from the RNG, I highly recommend War of the Omens as a free alternative.

If you're not as particular about that, if you like good art and atmosphere, or if you just want a decent timekill, Frost's developer is definitely still worth supporting. 10$ as an investment in a decent game and the hope of better games to come would not be a bad thing, and maybe they'll lean less on randomization and more on player choice.

[h1]Certainly not a game for everyone, but if you're intrigued by the theme or the thought of pushing your luck in a hostile card-driven affair, then Frost is a pretty cool pick.[/h1]

Aside from being chromatically challenged, Frost is notable for being a solitaire experience inspired by real world deck-building card games such as Dominion and its subsequent imitators including World of Tanks: Rush and Resident Evil.

The action, such as it is, takes place in the sort of post-apocalyptic setting that author Kurt Vonnegut made popular in his seminal novel Cat's Cradle; a freezing world where tribes must now band together for their very survival. In the game's 'Classic' mode you become a leader who must collect the resources needed to traverse the land in search of a mythical place called the "Refuge" whilst also trying your best to outrun the titular snow storm that threatens to consume all.

Every concept is rendered in card form with your own personal deck consisting of resources like Food, Materials, Survivors, and other gubbins such as weapons or even Ideas. Other cards stand in for the Regions that you must cross as well as the special events or obstacles that your tribe will run into along the way.

Also rearing its ugly head here is the time-worn mechanic by where a useless card (in this case representing Fatigue) is routinely dumped into your deck as play progresses. As with The Big Book of Madness, the inclusion of bogus cards makes thematic sense here because it's important for the player to feel pressured.

Nevertheless, I'm generally not a fan of mechanics like these and whilst Frost does offer you the default option of Resting in order to remove Fatigue, I really dislike how it's included in your starting deck. There are times when my first turn is skipped in order to remove Fatigue and that just feels wrong. Fatigue can also be incurred when activating certain cards that grant a random reward. Specialist cards like Supplies, the Gatherer or the Frigomancer are made very unattractive due to this foible and the same applies for when it's time to scavenge.

Scavenging is a necessary evil early on when your tribe lacks the resources required to physically pass into the next Region. By discarding a Survivor card, players run the risk of gaining Fatigue or killing the Survivor (!) for a chance at discovering Food, Materials, or other Survivors. These random draws can be of critical importance and yet Fatigue or fatalities can quickly pile up before you have a chance to really get going. When you consider that Regions and Ideas are also randomly generated, it only makes sense to continue harder games when the first round conditions are beneficial. In short: you can expect to be pressing the 'Restart' button a lot.

Many things are governed by random elements in fact, even down to certain card abilities that have a percentage chance of activating. You can spend time building a Trap, but that doesn't necessarily mean anything tasty is going to fall into it. To a degree this actually makes good thematic sense, but again it's the element of chance here that can make formulating reliable combo chains and other tactics next to impossible. It's this facet of Frost's design that's going to be the most taxing on your patience.

You lose the game when the Frost timer ticks down from eight to zero, and whilst the timer ticks up every time you travel onwards, it's extremely unlikely that your deck will contain the goods needed to do this consistently. One one hand this makes the game remarkably tense and the designer's unsubtle use of creepy music and jarring screen effects only enhance that tension further. Because of the reliance on randomization, however, Frost is a supremely difficult game to get to grips with and that hard time only continues to get harder as new cards and scenarios are unlocked.

Scenario play is more interesting than the Classic mode as in addition to collecting items or seeking out the Refuge, your scenario character will have goals of their own. The Hunter and The Meditator for example have simple objectives, but some like The Shadow and The Skeptic have quite involved missions with fresh patterns of play. Mixing this up further is the addition of character abilities that give each leader their own unique advantages and play styles.

The other thing about Scenarios is that they're hard. Really hard. And it's likely that most players' luck and patience will simply run out before they can achieve victory in each one. Part of the problem here once again revolves around the game's inherent randomness.

The developer has taken care not to label Frost as an actual deck-building game because of the false implication that you're in any way building an engine out of the cards that you collect. Getting the cards you desperately need to make your deck work is a process governed by chance and smoothed over via careful play. You're not so much building a deck as you are managing an ever-changing pool of resources, so there are times when defeat is going to be an inevitable outcome of drawing poorly and falling behind.

What's nice though is that Frost's intense difficulty is built up gradually as the player continues to finish games. By the time your card album is complete, you'll have discovered all sorts of new tools including stacked resources, Charisma checks, and as the result of several free updates; cards for Pets and Weather effects. With this breadth of content comes a sharper learning curve, but the on-screen tooltips and instructional blurbs are usually on point in explaining exactly what you need to know about each of the game's symbols.

Which brings us to Frost's rather wonderful presentation. It's certainly not one for photophobics, mind, but the all-white menus and eerie music do a near perfect job of transporting you into the setting. Also notable is the game's artwork whose roughshod charm resembles the works of Quentin Blake quite nicely. Story threads are limited to whatever awkwardly translated text you see during splash screens, which is a shame, but the overall theme of the "Frost" meaning different things to different people is an intriguing one nonetheless.

Despite its light and addictively simple gameplay then, Frost is not really a game for casual players. The real meat is found in the Scenarios and yet the sheer difficulty and trial and error nature of that mode is likely to frustrate those who go in unprepared.

Nevertheless, I'm currently finding this to be an equally difficult game to put down. Whether it's my intense fondness of card games or a hidden masochism that's responsible, I've taken great pleasure in exploring the bleak and uncompromising world that Frost represents.

Brutal singleplayer deckbuilder with a unique and beautiful art style. It's really its own beast- it doesn't play like your typical deckbuilder, but has its own ebb and flow that I find very satisfying.

Here's the basic game flow- you start with a handful of food and wood, and a couple survivors. You use your survivors to gain more resources, which you'll need to gain idea cards and to pass the area. Ideas are extremely useful and give you better access to resources, thin your deck, or remove negative cards. On the other hand, you only have a limited amount of time total to bypass a certain number of areas, so you can't usually dawdle around and just build a lot of ideas. But if you don't build enough ideas, then you'll be doomed when a particularly difficult area arises. 

Each area also has an encounter- sometimes friendly, sometimes not. Not all encounters are difficult, but they always throw a wrinkle in your plan.

You're always pushed forwards, but additional ideas are unlocked for each turn you stay in an area. It's often a difficult decision- do I stall for a turn or two to gain an excellent card, or do I forge onwards and hope it doesn't matter? The right choice isn't always obvious for a couple of areas, so learning what sorts of threats are likely to be ahead of you matters.

Additionally, more interesting cards and obstacles and areas are unlocked as you play. It's really a fascinating game, and there's nothing quite like it.

I bought it on sale, but I would argue it's worth the full price if card games are your thing.

Depuis la sortie du jeu sur table Dominion, différents jeux vidéo ont vu le jour mettant en scène un deck (pour les non initiés, un paquet de cartes) qui va contenir différentes ressources et actions que vous allez modifier au gré de l'aventure. A contrario des classiques où l'on affronte un adversaire, dans ce type de jeux, c'est l'environnement que l'on doit vaincre.

Dans Frost, votre objectif principal est de devancer le froid glacial synonyme de mort s'il vous rattrape. Pour ce faire, votre deck va contenir des provisions, du bois, des survivants et des idées que vous achèterez probablement au cours de la partie. Les icônes sont assez parlantes mais il est vivement conseillé de passer par le tutorial avant de lancer votre première partie.

Les cartes sont assez bien équilibrées et les différents scénarios ainsi que les nouvelles cartes qui se rajoutent viennent renouveler le gameplay et ajouter de la durée de vie.

Niveau graphisme on a quelque chose de simple dans des tons de blanc et bleu pour refletter le froid omniprésent dans l'aventure. De même au niveau audio on a quelque chose de très léger mais qui colle parfaitement à l'ambiance du jeu à savoir une tribu qui se bat dans une immensité glacée.

Personnellement, j'apprécie énormément ce type de jeu et de fait Frost a été une excellente surprise. Si vous êtes curieux ou que vous hésitez à l'acheter, je vous invite à essayer la démo et à vous faire votre propre opinion.
